solarSystems.subtitle: Understand the differences between solar PV system types to match your power needs, location, and budget.

items.name: On-Grid (Grid-Tied)
items.description: A solar PV system connected to the utility grid. Solar energy powers daytime loads, while excess or shortfall can be exported to or imported from the grid (subject to local regulations).
points: Reduces electricity bills by using solar power during the day
Lower upfront cost since batteries are typically not required
Usually does not supply power during grid outages (for safety), unless equipped with special backup/battery features
Best for homes and businesses with stable grid access

items.name: Off-Grid (Standalone)
items.description: A standalone solar PV system not connected to the utility grid. All energy is stored in batteries for use anytime, including at night.
points: Operates fully independently without relying on the utility grid
Ideal for remote locations or areas without grid access
Requires a battery bank and proper capacity management
Higher upfront investment due to batteries and controls

items.name: Hybrid (Grid + Battery)
items.description: A combination of on-grid and off-grid systems: connected to the utility grid and equipped with batteries for storage and backup power.
points: Can power critical loads during grid outages (backup)
Maximizes solar self-consumption and manages import/export of power
More flexible for changing needs (self-consumption & backup)
Higher cost and installation complexity than on-grid systems

care.subtitle: Most premature failures trace back to a handful of causes that good installation and maintenance practice can avoid.

items.title: Poor Lubrication
items.description: Too little, too much, or the wrong lubricant causes heat and wear. Follow the correct type and interval.

items.title: Contamination
items.description: Dirt and moisture damage raceways. Effective sealing and clean handling extend life significantly.

items.title: Incorrect Mounting
items.description: Hammering, misalignment, or wrong fits cause early damage. Use proper tools and heating methods.

items.title: Electrical Damage
items.description: Current passing through a bearing can cause fluting. Consider insulation or grounding on drive motors.

items.q: How do I find the right replacement bearing?
items.a: Start with the number printed on the old bearing. If it is unreadable, measure the bore, outside diameter, and width, and note the type and any seals. Send us those details and we will match it.

items.q: What is the difference between ZZ and 2RS?
items.a: ZZ bearings have metal shields that do not touch the inner ring, giving lower friction and higher speed capability. 2RS bearings have rubber contact seals that better exclude dust and moisture, with slightly more friction.

items.q: When should I choose C3 clearance?
items.a: C3 is common in electric motors and applications with interference fits or higher operating temperatures, because the bearing loses some clearance when fitted and heated. Check the equipment specification.

items.q: Can I use a different brand as a replacement?
items.a: Generally yes, since bearings follow standard dimensions. Confirm that the type, size, clearance, seal, and cage suit the application, as internal design can vary between manufacturers.

items.q: Can I mix different lubricant brands or types?
items.a: It is best to avoid it. Different additive packages and base oils can be incompatible and reduce performance. If a change is needed, follow a proper flush and changeover procedure.

items.q: How often should industrial oil be changed?
items.a: There is no single interval. It depends on the equipment, operating conditions, and oil type. Condition-based changes guided by oil analysis are usually more cost-effective than fixed schedules.

items.q: What is the difference between mineral and synthetic oils?
items.a: Mineral oils are refined from crude oil and suit most standard conditions. Synthetic oils offer better stability at extreme temperatures and often longer drain intervals, at a higher purchase price.

items.q: How do I know which grease NLGI grade to use?
items.a: NLGI 2 is the most common for general bearings. Softer grades suit centralized systems and low temperatures, while firmer grades suit high-speed or vertical applications. Confirm with the OEM.

items.q: How do I choose the right hydraulic hose?
items.a: Determine working pressure (including impulses), inside diameter, temperature, media type, installation space, and end connection type. Then select the appropriate construction and standard. If unsure, send us specifications or a sample of your old hose.

items.q: What is the difference between 1SN and 2SN hoses?
items.a: 1SN has one layer of steel wire braid, while 2SN has two. For the same diameter, 2SN generally has a higher working pressure.

items.q: When should I use a PTFE hose?
items.a: Choose PTFE for high temperatures, aggressive chemicals, or cleanliness requirements such as in food and pharmaceutical industries. For general hydraulics on heavy equipment, wire braid or wire spiral is usually more suitable.

items.q: Can I mix hoses and fittings from different manufacturers?
items.a: It is not recommended. Hose, fitting, and crimp data are specified by the manufacturer. Mixing components without official data can reduce safety and working pressure of the assembly.

items.q: How long does a hydraulic hose last?
items.a: There is no fixed lifespan as it depends heavily on pressure, temperature, movement, and environment. Perform regular inspections and replace if there are leaks, cover cracks, bulges, or visible reinforcement wires.

items.q: Can I order a hose assembly with custom length and fittings?
items.a: Yes. Send us the hose type, length, fitting types and angles, or a sample of the old assembly. We will prepare an assembly to those specifications.
